title: Notes that sync across your devices
like: a private offline notebook like Standard Notes
brief: Build a notebook that works on a phone and laptop, including a month offline. Edits should reach connected foreground devices in under a second, concurrent work must not disappear, and the server should not need plaintext notes. Push wakes devices; durable sync must work when push does not.

clarify.a: The note edit and device outbox operation are committed locally before the screen says saved on this device. Synced means the server durably accepted the operation. Losing the device before sync remains a real data-loss boundary.

Use stable operation ids and base versions. Preserve concurrent whole-note edits as conflict versions in the first release. Do not silently pick by wall time. A text CRDT is a possible later choice with a tested merge policy.

clarify.q: How long can a device be away?
clarify.a: Support 30 days. Keep deletion history for 90 days with a documented margin. Older cursors require snapshot rebase and version-checked replay of preserved local edits. A stale full upload must not resurrect a deletion.

Encrypt note bodies on devices. The server stores ciphertext and minimal routing metadata. Search is local. Device enrollment, revocation and an explicit recovery key are part of the design. Server KMS protects metadata only; it does not hold note decryption keys.

requirements.users: 1 million people with about 3 devices each (approx.)
notes: Each sync operation carries about 1 KB. A notebook has 10,000 notes of about 2 KB each; one pull finds 50 changed notes. Keep tombstones for 90 days and support devices offline for 30 days (approx.).
Under-a-second is a foreground connected-device goal. Background push and offline devices have eventual delivery. The scored notify path measures sender acceptance, not device receipt.

The graph carries encrypted operations and small reads. It does not implement offline storage, conflict resolution, cursors, end-to-end encryption, recovery or tombstones. A traffic pass does not prove these properties.
KMS and audit nodes protect server metadata and record content-free access/deletion receipts. They are not the end-to-end content key service.
The 900 ms target measures one request. Subsecond propagation needs an end-to-end budget across commit, change notification, pull and local application; a traffic pass does not verify it.
Sources emit only their assigned request types. The source rates below reproduce the aggregate workload; protocol guarantees still require the separate design checkpoint.

Scored data retention: at least 90 days on active authoritative stores. Copies used only for search or reports can be rebuilt. Local device history and rollup policies still require the separate protocol check.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

workloadPlan.role: encrypted device operations, pulls and wake requests

text.name: Synchronized rush
text.description: Many callers send requests together instead of spreading them over time.

debrief.headline: A synchronized rush hit {node}.
debrief.fix: Spread scheduled work over time and keep spare capacity on the affected path. A rate limiter protects downstream work by rejecting excess calls, so it cannot by itself meet every availability target.

numbers.label: Peak edit payload
numbers.how: 3,000 × 0.6 × 1 KB, before replica and metadata work (approx.).

numbers.label: Delta payload for 50 changed notes
numbers.how: 50 × 2 KB; versus 10,000 × 2 KB = 20 MB for a full notebook (approx.).

numbers.label: Deletion history margin
numbers.how: 90-day tombstones - 30-day supported offline period; old cursors still need explicit rebase.

hints: What must be committed locally before a network request, and what does a sync cursor acknowledge?
Use stable ids, atomic local edit-plus-outbox, durable server deduplication and version checks. Push is only a wake hint.
Tombstones, key lifecycle and producer epochs must prevent resurrection. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Each device has an encrypted local database, a transactionally written outbox and a committed pull cursor. The server authenticates devices, deduplicates tenant-scoped operation ids, saves ciphertext and an event in one transaction, and returns the accepted version without moving the device's pull cursor past unseen remote edits. Connected clients pull deltas; a wake worker uses the durable server outbox and retries push. The reference models the authority and push sender as separate requests through the API. It does not pretend the sim verifies their transactional relationship.

designs.name: Encrypted operations with a synchronous authority
designs.why: A multi-zone SQL authority can store operation ids, versions, tombstones and the durable server outbox together. Immediate pulls use the authority for read-your-writes. Notify requests represent dispatch after an outbox job becomes due; the API fleet includes that dispatcher role. There is no database-to-push wire because the database does not make network calls. Direct dispatch in the graph measures sender capacity, not atomic outbox publication.

tradeoffs: Conflict copies are easier to explain and test than arbitrary text merging, but users must resolve them. A CRDT can reduce manual conflicts at the cost of metadata, compaction rules and editor-specific semantics.

End-to-end encryption moves search and key handling to devices. Recovery needs an authorized device or a recovery secret; password reset alone cannot reconstruct content keys. Metadata still leaks timing and sizes.

Tombstones cannot expire independently of the supported offline horizon and replica repair. Devices returning beyond the horizon need a fresh snapshot, with unsynced work preserved and base versions validated. After tombstones expire, reject old epochs or unknown base versions; a fresh snapshot alone does not make stale queued uploads safe.

A push acknowledgement is not device delivery. Durable cursors, retries and periodic or foreground pulls recover missed wakes. Batching reduces radio wakeups; attachment sync can prefer charging and Wi-Fi.
Deletion jobs cover ciphertext versions, local indexes, caches, object attachments and backups under a stated deadline. Revoking a device cannot erase plaintext it already copied.
editorial.realWorld: A 10,000-note notebook at 2 KB/note is about 20 MB. Fifty changed notes cost about 100 KB before metadata, about 200 times less payload. Local changes can feel instant while network synchronization remains pending (approx.).

correctness.prompt: A month-old laptop uploads an edited note that the phone deleted. How do the cursor, base version and tombstone keep the deletion from silently disappearing?
correctness.discussion: Keep a durable local edit and operation id while pulling server changes. A tombstone identifies the deleted note and version. The server validates the edit base version, then preserves a conflict or requests user resolution instead of treating an old snapshot as truth. If history expired, download a new snapshot without discarding local unsynced operations and rebase them explicitly. Use stable ids across retries. Commit cursor advancement with local application of the pulled changes. Content encryption and key recovery require separate endpoint tests. Upload acknowledgement and pull progress are separate. A server-assigned upload version is not evidence that earlier remote changes have been downloaded. Ciphertext transport does not solve concurrent edit semantics. Push is a wakeup signal, not the durable synchronization log. Tombstones, key lifecycle and producer epochs must prevent resurrection.

fields.label: Step 1. Phone and laptop edit the same note after a month offline. What survives?
options: Both causal operations under a specified merge or visible conflict policy
Whichever ciphertext reached the server last
fields.explanation: Ciphertext transport does not solve concurrent edit semantics.

fields.label: Step 2. Push delivery is lost. How does the laptop discover changes?
options: Durable cursor-based sync with versioned encrypted operations
fields.explanation: Push is a wakeup signal, not the durable synchronization log.

fields.label: Step 3. An old device uploads after account deletion. What happens?
options: Reject the old deletion epoch and verify retained copy cleanup under the offline policy
Recreate the account from its encrypted upload
fields.explanation: Tombstones, key lifecycle and producer epochs must prevent resurrection.

correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.
correctness.responsibility: Merge encrypted offline edits and propagate deletion without relying on push.
